q: A heat engine is a system that converts heat to _____ energy.
e: A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so it can do mechanical work. It repeats a cycle so work keeps coming out. Turning work into heat is dissipation, not this engine. Heat engine is a system that converts cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: A series of processes in which a system is brought back to its initial state is called a _____.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of work output to _____.
e: Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H. You can also write 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Heat input over work output is the reciprocal, not the efficiency. Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Applying the first law to one complete cycle of a heat engine, the net change of internal energy $\Delta U$ is _____.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. f-numbers in this chapter are positive ratios.

q: The transformation of heat into work is usually accomplished by the internal combustion engine and the _____ engine.
e: Practical heat-into-work machines are internal combustion engines and steam engines. In both, a gas in a cylinder is taken around a cycle. Nuclear or solar plants are different textbook chapters.

q: In a gasoline engine, the combustion of the mixture takes place explosively by an _____.
e: A gasoline engine intakes fuel plus air and ignites with an electric spark. Four piston motions are the strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead intakes air only and auto-ignites injected fuel. Efficiency is W over Q_H.

q: The gasoline engine cycle involves processes where four require motion of the piston and are called _____.
e: Four piston motions in the gasoline cycle are the strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Spark ignition happens between compression and power, at nearly constant volume. Diesel still has strokes but intakes air only. A gasoline engine intakes fuel plus air and ignites with an electric spark.

q: During the intake stroke, a mixture is drawn into the cylinder by the _____ stroke of the piston.
e: On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air. Diesel intake draws air only. Compression then raises p and T of whatever was drawn in. Intake stroke a mixture is drawn into cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In a gasoline engine, the volume remains unchanged and the piston does not move during the _____ process.

q: The theoretical efficiency of a gasoline engine depends on the compression ratio and the ratio of _____ heat capacities.

Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air.

e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. Efficiency is W over Q_H.

q: In 1824, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical engine known as the _____ engine.
e: In 1824 Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical reversible engine between two reservoirs. That Carnot engine sets the upper efficiency bound for every real engine on the same pair of temperatures. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. Friction and irreversibility make real engines worse.

q: The Carnot engine operates on an ideal reversible cycle between _____ heat reservoirs.
e: The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

e: Heat-engine efficiency is work out divided by heat in, W/Q_H or 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Carnot replaces the heat ratio with T_C/T_H on an absolute scale. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. The reciprocal, heat in over work out, is not efficiency.

q: All real engines are less efficient than the Carnot engine because they do not operate through a _____ cycle.

q: In a reversible process, the system can be returned to its initial condition along the same path on the _____ diagram.
e: In a reversible process you can return along the same p-V path to the start. Infinitesimally slow is the main thermodynamic condition. An irreversible process cannot retrace that path. A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly.

q: Carnot's theorem states that no engine can be more efficient than a _____ engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: Carnot's theorem: no engine between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine on those reservoirs. The corollary is that all reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. Different efficiencies mean irreversibility or different temperatures.
